stops.name: Pensacola, the birth on the Gulf coast
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the date 28 December 1940 comes from Wikidata Q2395889 and from jordanmaxwellshow.com, with a FamilySearch profile (GLRL-XSG) carrying the Pensacola birthplace. No birth certificate, obituary, or census entry has been produced by anyone, and the Euro Weekly News notice of his death gives his age as 82, which does not fit this date. City-level coordinate only.
stops.campa: On the Gulf coast of Florida a son is born to the Pine family and named Russell Joseph. Nothing else of the birth survives in any record anyone has produced: no hospital, no street, no certificate, no attending name. The genealogical profiles and the memorial pages that carry the December date agree with one another and rest on one another, which is not the same thing as agreeing with a document. He will spend six decades telling audiences that institutions bury their own beginnings, and his own beginning is a line in a database.
sources: ancestors.familysearch.org profile GLRL-XSG (fetch returned a browser-compatibility page only)

stops.name: Los Angeles, the Complete Books of Charles Fort
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from interview-derived biography; the year is inferred from his own statement that he was about nineteen, and the day and month are placeholders. No contemporaneous record of the move exists, and the man named in every retelling as Bob Ferney appears in no source of any kind.
stops.campa: At about nineteen he comes west to Los Angeles with almost no money. An acquaintance the retellings call Bob Ferney puts into his hands The Complete Books of Charles Fort: rains of frogs, falls of stone, lights over the sea, an enormous catalogue of things the sciences had filed and then declined to look at. Fort called them damned facts, excluded not because they were disproved but because they did not fit. The young man takes the four volumes as a working method rather than a curiosity. Collect what the institutions drop; then ask who benefits from the dropping.
sources: Interview-derived secondary biographies summarized in the research dossier
suggested_refs: Charles Fort, The Book of the Damned (1919), first volume of the omnibus he is said to have been given

stops.name: Los Angeles, the year he dates it from
stops.date_confidence: attested as a self-report: his own site gives 1959 and nothing narrower, so the month is a placeholder chosen to sit after the arrival stop. The claim is his, and no independent record of research activity in 1959 exists.

segments.name: The Seminar Circuit: Los Angeles, 1989 to 1992

stops.name: Los Angeles, the seminars begin
stops.date_confidence: attested only in his own promotional biography, which gives the year without a month; day and month are placeholders. No independent corporate filing for United Sensitives of America has been located.
stops.campa: He begins holding regular seminars in Los Angeles and takes a seat on the board of directors of a body called United Sensitives of America. The room is the unit of the work now: a rented hall, a slide carousel, three or four hours on the symbols cut into public buildings and printed on currency. He does not publish first and lecture after. He lectures, is taped, and the tapes go out through mail order and swap. The audience is assembled cassette by cassette. Nothing of his reaches a bookshop for another eleven years.

The building on South Ardmore Avenue, which will one day be given over to a legal charity for the poor, is a radio house of the old kind: transmitters, carpet, a lit sign over the door.

No initiation record for him exists in any jurisdiction, and later admirers will circulate a claim that he held the thirty-second degree; the claim has no document behind it. segments.name: 1994 and 1995: Expos, Campuses, and the Dark Side of Religion

stops.name: Los Angeles, the KABC rotation
stops.date_confidence: his bio lists three KABC appearances, in 1994, 1995 and 1996, none with a month; the date here is a placeholder for the run. Coordinate is 3321 La Cienega Boulevard, KABC's studios of the period.
stops.campa: Three separate bookings on KABC across three years: the Ray Briem show with the newsman Bill Jenkins as co-guest, then Jenkins hosting him alone on Main Street America for two shows, then two hours with Doug Stephen. Los Angeles talk radio in these years runs all night and needs guests who can fill it, and he is reliable, unhurried, and never short of material. Between lecture tours this is what the work is: a chair, a headset, and a switchboard of callers asking about the eye on the dollar.

stops.name: Burbank, the antiquarian book fair
stops.date_confidence: listed in his own chronology as May 1994 with no venue named; the coordinate approximates Burbank's convention-centre district and is not a confirmed fair address.
stops.campa: He appears at an antiquarian book fair in Burbank, among dealers in first editions and foxed nineteenth-century plates. This is the other half of him, the half the expo circuit does not show: a collector and reseller of old comparative-mythology books, Gerald Massey and Godfrey Higgins and the Victorian Egyptologists, most of them out of print for a century. His lectures are largely a rereading of these volumes aloud for an audience that will never see them. The trade in old books is also, for years, part of how he earns.
suggested_refs: Gerald Massey, A Book of the Beginnings (1881), and Godfrey Higgins, Anacalypsis (1836), the two Victorian sources his astrotheology leans on hardest

It is the most conventional room he ever addresses. The booking survives only because he listed it himself, in a line that puts the hotel in the wrong city.

stops.name: Los Angeles, the campus month
stops.date_confidence: his chronology lists UCLA, USC and Ventura College all in March 1995 without days; the day here orders the stop after the Dreamland broadcast. The coordinate is UCLA. The Ventura College talk carried the title 'The Story the Church Didn't Tell You!' and ran three hours.
stops.campa: In a single month he speaks at UCLA, at USC, and at Ventura College up the coast. Student unions book him the way they book any speaker who will draw a full room on a weeknight; he arrives with slides and stays for questions until the janitors want the hall. Nothing about these bookings makes him a member of a faculty, and nothing in any registrar's file makes him a graduate of anywhere. He is a lecturer in the oldest sense of the word: a man paid for an evening.

Three hours is the length he prefers, long enough to build the whole chain of etymologies in front of an audience. His own chronology puts the university in the wrong city. Which half of the entry is wrong, the town or the school, cannot be settled from anything on the page.

segments.name: The Books and the Federal Case

stops.name: Los Angeles, Matrix of Power
stops.date_confidence: the book is catalogued by Open Library as a single Book Tree edition dated 2000, with no month; the publisher's address is not carried here, so the coordinate is his own base. The page citations below are to the scanned copy on archive.org.
stops.campa: The lectures become a book at last. Matrix of Power is thin, plainly printed, and assembled out of talks, and it does what the tapes could not: it fixes sentences in a form that can be quoted and checked. The famous passage on the bankers who run the government turns out, on the page, to be him quoting a mayor of New York from 1922 rather than speaking in his own voice, with one sentence of his own attached to it. Eighty pages later comes the line that outlives everything else he wrote.

stops.name: Los Angeles, That Old-Time Religion
stops.date_confidence: the second Book Tree title of 2000, written with Paul Tice and Alan Snow; no month is recorded, and the day here orders it after Matrix of Power. Coordinate is his own base rather than the publisher's address.
stops.campa: The second book of the year sets out the argument entire: that the Christian story is the solar year told as biography, that the twelve who follow Jesus are the twelve signs, and that the church was built by men who understood the allegory and taught it as history to people who did not. It is not an original thesis and he does not claim it is; it is the Victorian comparative mythologists rewritten for a paperback audience. He adds one practical conclusion of his own, and states it as advice.
stops.quote: Gnosis in Greek means knowledge, or to know. This does not refer to factual knowledge, but to an intuitive or spiritual understanding that comes from experience. The early Gnostics were mystics, people who knew that you could experience God for yourself instead of going into a church and being told what to believe. In Hebrew, to know means to experience, so, according to the Hebrews, knowing God means to experience Him. This is what most all early Hebrews and Christians were striving to do. Unfortunately, the Church got in the way of personal experience, by creating "organized religion." There's a saying which states, "Religion is for the masses, and mysticism is for the individual." If you want to be a sheep and follow along with the masses to get a generic, candy-coated version of your spirituality, then follow the teachings of the Christian fathers. If you want to explore your own individual spirituality, you must go deeply inside yourself, instead of through church doors.
stops.quote_source: Jordan Maxwell, Paul Tice and Alan Snow, That Old-Time Religion: The Story of Religious Foundations (Book Tree, 2000)

stops.name: Los Angeles, the default judgment
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Memorandum Decision was signed by Judge Nora M. Manella on 27 April 2004 and filed the 28th, with the FTC posting the default judgment and permanent injunction under 17 June 2004. The clerk's entry of default came earlier, in January 2004, after service by publication in the Los Angeles Times.
stops.campa: He never appears. Served at last through a notice in the Los Angeles Times, he lets the default stand, and the court decides the case on the government's papers alone. The judgment enjoins him permanently and holds him and his co-defendant jointly liable for the whole of what the customers paid, computed to the cent. No criminal charge is ever brought and no conviction exists. There is only the civil number, and it follows the name for the rest of his life.

segments.name: Egypt, Malta, and the Voice That Travels Without Him

stops.name: Giza, the Ancient Wisdom tour
stops.date_confidence: his chronology lists a 2004 Egypt tour without months or days; the date here is a placeholder chosen to sit after the April judgment, and nothing establishes the actual season. Whether he personally attended or was only billed has not been independently confirmed. Coordinate is the Giza plateau.
stops.campa: Five years after the first tour he is back on the plateau, in the same year in which the federal judgment lands against him in Los Angeles. The group format has settled by now: a coach, a dozen or two travellers, evenings of talks in a hotel room with the pyramids lit up beyond the window, and a morning at the Sphinx enclosure before the coaches arrive. He is sixty-three and this is the third of four Egyptian journeys. Whether he was on this particular coach or only on the brochure is not something the surviving paper can answer.

stops.name: Malta, the megalithic temples
stops.date_confidence: his chronology gives 'PQI Events 2006 Q3 International Conference, Malta, Radisson SAS Golden Sands, February 25 to March 5, 2006', naming the hotel and no temple. Hagar Qim stands here for the island's megalithic sites as a representative landmark, not as a confirmed itinerary stop.
stops.campa: Nine days in Malta with a conference party based at a resort on the northwest coast, and on the island the oldest free-standing stone buildings anyone has found, older than the pyramids by a thousand years. Hagar Qim faces the sunrise of the summer solstice through a hole cut in a slab. Religion, in his account, begins as an accurate record of the sky, and these temples are the strongest evidence he ever stands in front of. They are also the hardest to build a conspiracy out of. Nobody knows who raised them, or what they said.
suggested_refs: The Hagar Qim and Mnajdra temple complex, Qrendi, Malta

stops.name: Giza, the eclipse tour
stops.date_confidence: his chronology gives 25 March to 6 April 2006 for the tour, described elsewhere as a solar-eclipse trip. The total eclipse of 29 March 2006 crossed Egypt; his presence on the ground is attested only by his own listing.
stops.campa: Three weeks after Malta he is in Egypt again, this time for the eclipse. On the twenty-ninth of March the moon covers the sun over the western desert and the sky goes to dusk at midmorning. He has spent forty years telling audiences that the ancients organised their whole religion around this body and its disappearances, that the dying and rising god is the sun and always was. He stands in the shadow of the thing itself. It is his fourth and last recorded journey to Egypt.
suggested_refs: The total solar eclipse of 29 March 2006, path of totality across the Egyptian western desert

stops.name: Los Angeles, his voice in the opening of Zeitgeist
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia's article on the film gives the online release of 18 June 2007 and names the audio quotations from Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche, Jordan Maxwell and George Carlin. The coordinate is his own base, because the film was made and released without him present at either; he travelled nowhere for this.
stops.campa: A young filmmaker in New York cuts a film out of found footage and posts it free on the internet, and the opening montage carries three voices. One of them is his. The first part of the film is his own thesis, the gospel read as a solar calendar, delivered to an audience of millions who have never heard of an expo hall in Los Angeles. Neither the seminars nor the books nor thirty years of tape reached a fraction of the people this reaches in a season, and he is paid nothing for it and controls none of it. He is sixty-six, and he travelled nowhere to be in it.

stops.name: Los Angeles, signing over the name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the assignment of 30 March 2010 is described in the later trademark record and litigation, but the signed document itself was not obtained in this research. Neither the place of signature nor the circumstances are established, so the coordinate is his own base.
stops.campa: Russell Joseph Pine, signing as Jordan Maxwell, assigns the copyrights, the trademarks, and the domain names attached to the name Jordan Maxwell to a man called Josef Dolezal. He is sixty-nine and the archive is forty years of tape, video, and out-of-print paper. He thinks he is signing a business arrangement with a man who will handle the selling for him. Lawyers reading it later find that the name itself has changed hands. No copy of the signed instrument has since been produced; it survives as a recital in other people's filings.

stops.name: Los Angeles, the Court of Appeal
stops.date_confidence: attested: Maxwell v. Dolezal, B254893, decided 4 November 2014 by the Second District, Division Seven, published at 231 Cal.App.4th 93. Coordinate is the Ronald Reagan State Building, seat of the Second District. Note that the opinion contains no reference whatever to the FTC action, contrary to a citation in circulation.
stops.campa: He sues Dolezal in state court without a lawyer, and the trial court throws the case out. On appeal the court splits the difference in a way that decides nothing he wanted decided: his claim over the use of his own name and likeness fails, because he consented to exactly that in 2010 and the document says so, while his claim that the contract was broken is allowed to go back for trial. The opinion is a ruling about pleading, not about who was wronged. No record located shows what happened on remand.
sources: Maxwell v. Dolezal, 231 Cal.App.4th 93 (Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist., Div. 7, 4 November 2014), full text via the Caselaw Access Project

stops.name: Alexandria, the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board reverses
stops.date_confidence: attested: In re Momentum Development LLC, Ser. No. 85826122, decision mailed 6 September 2017. The docket was terminated on 20 December 2017 and the registration, No. 5377518, did not issue until 16 January 2018; the three dates are routinely conflated into one.
stops.campa: The examining attorney had refused the application, because a living person's name cannot be registered as a mark without that person's written consent, and Jordan Maxwell was alive and objecting. The board reads the 2010 assignment and finds the consent inside it: a document transferring everything cannot sensibly be read as withholding the one thing that makes the transfer worth having. The refusal is reversed. Four months later the registration issues. The name he made for himself, and worked under for fifty years, is a trademark belonging to a company.

stops.name: California, the death announced on a Wednesday
stops.date_confidence: 23 March 2022 is the announcement date given by Euro Weekly News and the death date recorded at Wikidata Q2395889; no death certificate, coroner report, or family obituary has been produced. The paper gives his age as 82 and the memorial pages as 81, following the 1940 birth year. No city, institution, or cause is named by any source, and the coordinate is a placeholder for his Southern California base.
stops.campa: The news moves the way everything about him moved, through tribute posts and forum threads and a broadcast remembrance, and a photograph of an old man in a hospital bed circulates without a hospital attached to it. No certificate has surfaced. No cemetery, no funeral home, no plot. Two websites announce the death of the same man and disagree about his age. He is eighty-one, or eighty-two, in California, or somewhere in California, on a date that is really the date the internet found out.
